summary: Describes a solution for customers of a single ISP who use BGP4 but do not need their own allocated AS, following RFC 1930. The provider can use a dedicated AS for such sites. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some small customers use a routing system that needs an ID number. This lets a provider share one ID among many small customers instead of giving each their own.

subtitle: How service providers can use a shared AS number for single-homed BGP customers.

tldr.problem: RFC 1930 recommends that autonomous systems (AS numbers) be allocated only when needed. However, BGP4 requires an AS number, and some single-homed customers (those with one internet connection) need BGP for load-sharing or dynamic prefix advertisement, creating a conflict with allocation guidelines.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of allocating a unique AS number to each small customer, an ISP can designate one AS number (from private space or a previously allocated block) for all such single-homed customers. Logically, the ISP has many peers with the same AS, but they are isolated islands with no direct connections between them.
tldr.outcome: ISPs can support single-homed customers needing BGP without consuming globally unique AS numbers, aligning with RFC 1930's philosophy. Customers understand they receive default routes and cannot see routes of other customers using the same shared AS.

facts.label: Typical use
facts.value: Single-homed customers needing load-sharing or dynamic prefixes

facts.label: Route visibility
facts.value: Default route only; cannot see other customers with same AS

today: RFC 2270 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains a practical solution for ISPs managing BGP sessions with single-homed customers, though it represents a trade-off between compliance with RFC 1930 allocation guidelines and operational flexibility.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
RFC 1930 sets guidelines for when organizations need an autonomous system (AS) number. It recommends that AS numbers be allocated only when truly necessary, such as when a site is multi-homed to multiple providers. However, practice has created exceptions: some single-homed customers (those connected to just one ISP) need to use BGP4 for practical reasons, even though they don't fit the RFC 1930 criteria.

Two scenarios drive this need: (1) Customers multi-homed to a single provider may need multiple BGP connections to that one ISP for redundancy and load-sharing; (2) Customers needing to advertise many different IP prefixes find it administratively easier to do so dynamically with BGP instead of manually configuring static routes.

RFC 2270 proposes a solution: the ISP allocates a single, dedicated AS number for all such single-homed BGP customers. Each customer uses the same AS number, but they are operationally isolated: no customer-to-customer routes leak between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Small customers connected to one company's network sometimes need BGP to manage their traffic. Instead of giving each a unique number, the provider assigns them all the same number.

sections.title: How the Dedicated AS Works
sections.content:
The dedicated AS is specified by the ISP and is purely for peering between the ISP and its customers. From the ISP's perspective, it has many BGP peers, all claiming the same AS number, but these peers are in isolated "islands" with no direct connections between them.

The ISP can use either a private AS number (from the range 64512 to 65535, defined in RFC 1930) or an AS previously allocated to the ISP itself. If a private AS is used, the ISP must strip it from routes before advertising them upstream, to prevent ambiguity in the global routing system.

Operationally, the solution is transparent: each customer configures BGP to peer with the ISP using the designated AS number, just as if it were their own unique AS. The ISP handles the fact that multiple customers use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider picks one ID number and gives it to all the small customers. When routes go to the rest of the internet, the ID is removed so there is no confusion.

sections.title: What Changes for Customers
sections.content:
Customers using a shared dedicated AS must understand several implications: (1) They cannot receive the full BGP routing table because of BGP loop detection. BGP rejects routes that contain the customer's own AS in the path, so a customer with AS number N cannot receive routes that AS N originated or passed through. This means customers cannot see routes from other customers using the same shared AS; (2) Customers must carry a default route from their ISP, as they cannot learn all routes directly.

However, these limitations are acceptable for single-homed sites. They typically only need routes to their own prefixes and default routing to the ISP, not a complete global routing table. The lack of routes from other customers using the same AS is inconsequential because those other customers are independent organizations.

If a customer's connectivity changes (e.g., moving to a different ISP or becoming multi-homed to multiple providers), they must reconfigure to use a different AS: either a globally unique one if multi-homed, or the dedicated AS of their new ISP if they become single-homed again.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers using the shared ID cannot see each other's routes because of how BGP prevents loops, but they only need their own routes and a default path anyway.

sections.title: Routing Registry and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The Internet Routing Registry (IRR) is used to create route filters and policy rules. With multiple customers using the same AS, finer granularity is needed. Providers can use additional attributes in route objects, such as the "mntner" (maintainer) or "community" attribute, alongside the AS number, to create filtering rules specific to each customer.

Route aggregation works in the provider's favor: because all customers using the dedicated AS are single-homed to the provider and receive addresses from the provider's CIDR block, the provider already originates the aggregated prefix. Individual customer prefixes do not need to be announced upstream, since the larger block covers them.

The solution assumes customers trust their ISP to manage the shared AS responsibly and that the ISP has the operational discipline to apply correct routing policies to each customer despite sharing an AS number.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider writes rules to keep customer traffic separate, and larger route announcements cover everyone without listing them individually.
